channel.title: Yusuf Gadelrab
channel.description: Building in public: AI tooling, CS education research, trading systems, and free tools.

item.title: TradingView vs TrendSpider vs Stock Rover: which one a swing trader actually needs
item.description: I wrote my own screener before I paid for anyone else's. That is the only reason this comparison is worth reading: I know which parts of these products do real work.

item.title: Koyfin vs Seeking Alpha vs Simply Wall St: what each one is actually for
item.description: Every list ranks these three against each other as if they do the same thing. One is a data terminal, one is an opinion marketplace, and one is a picture.

item.title: Which AI tools I pay for, and what I run locally for free instead
item.description: I run a 30-billion-parameter model on my own laptop and it costs nothing per token. That changes which AI subscriptions are worth paying for, and eliminates most.

item.title: How to check a repo for secrets before you make it public
item.description: Deleting an API key from a file does not delete it from your repository. It is still in the object store, and the moment you go public it is indexed.

item.title: The student software stack: what is free, and the four things worth paying for
item.description: Almost everything you are told to buy as a CS student is free for students, and most people never claim it because nobody hands you the list.

item.title: I built three apps this week and put zero of them in the App Store
item.description: The App Store costs $99/year. I'm a broke CS student. So I built them as PWAs instead: you open a link on your phone, hit Share, hit Add to Home Screen, and it's on your homescreen with an icon. Works offline. No account. No backend. Your data never leaves your phone because there is no server to se

item.title: I shipped a brand across 30 pages, 3 apps, 3 book covers and a clothing line in one day
item.description: Most brand systems are a folder of PNGs and a PDF nobody opens. The mark drifts. Someone exports it wrong for a t-shirt, the knockout becomes ink on ink, and six months later you have four versions of your own logo and no idea which is right.

item.title: I wrote a security scanner with zero dependencies, on purpose
item.description: Every security tool I looked at wanted me to install a hundred packages to go looking for supply chain risk. That struck me as funny in a way that isn't funny.

item.title: I spent a day making my portfolio readable by AI instead of by humans
item.description: Here's the thing I noticed. When a recruiter wants to know about a candidate now, a real number of them ask an assistant first. ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, whatever is in the search box. If the model can't parse you, you don't exist in that answer.

item.title: The hardest part of an internship search isn't the applications. It's that nobody tells you when it starts
item.description: I learned this the expensive way. Summer 2027 internship recruiting is happening right now, in July 2026. Not in the spring. Not in the fall. Now.

item.title: Two papers accepted to SIGCSE 2026. I'm an undergrad
item.description: The first one asks a question that sounds simple and isn't: what happens to a student learning to code when the programming language is in English and their thinking isn't?

item.title: How an undergrad with no connections gets into a research lab, specifically
item.description: I get asked this a lot now that I have two SIGCSE 2026 papers, so here is the actual sequence, not the inspirational version.

item.title: I built a visa timeline planner because I got tired of being scared of a calendar
item.description: I'm on TD status. It ends when I turn 21. I'm 20. There's a whole sequence of things that have to happen in a specific order before then, and every explanation of that sequence I could find was either a law firm's marketing page or a forum post from 2019.

item.title: I spent months building trading strategies and then published the results that killed most of them
item.description: Here's what walk-forward testing did to my ideas.

item.title: I skipped the App Store and shipped 3 offline PWAs instead. Here's what that actually costs you
item.description: Apple wants $99/year before a single person can install your thing. I'm a student, so I went the PWA route for three small apps and want to write down the honest tradeoffs, because every PWA post I read was either a fanboy or a funeral.

item.title: Zero-dependency security scanner: secrets, OSV CVEs, IaC rules, git-history leaks, SBOM
item.description: I got annoyed that scanning for supply chain risk usually means installing a large dependency tree first, so I wrote one with no dependencies at all. Pure stdlib Python, MIT.

item.title: Built a position size calculator that refuses to let you round up. Free, no signup
item.description: The single most expensive habit I had was sizing by feel and then rounding the share count up to something clean. 187 shares becomes 200 because 200 looks like a number. That rounding is a silent 7% increase in risk on every trade, and it compounds against you in exactly the periods you can least af
